paras: The whipping of a Black witness at Fort Myers was an assault on an unnamed Black man by several white men at Fort Myers, Florida, shortly before March 21, 1903. The only account comes from George L. Battersby, a deputy sheriff of DeSoto county, who said the man was punished for lying under oath at the inquest into the murder of the Punta Gorda marshal. No arrests were reported, and the deputy's explanation was printed as the story.

Marshal J. H. Bowman of Punta Gorda was murdered, and I. E. Cooper was later convicted of the crime and sentenced to death. An inquest into the killing was held at Punta Gorda, and according to Battersby the Black man testified there.

Battersby, who was also a candidate for marshal of Fort Myers, said the man had "deliberately swore to a lie that might have caused the lynching of several innocent men." In the deputy's telling, the man admitted when questioned that he had lied and said he did not know why, "unless it was because he was drunk." "Several white citizens," whom Battersby did not name, then decided the man "needed a lesson" and whipped him at Fort Myers. The exact date, the number of men involved and the extent of his injuries are not given.

The coverage shows no arrests, inquiry or charges over the whipping. In July 1904 a preliminary hearing at Arcadia discharged a Battersby and a Windham who had been charged with complicity in Bowman's murder, though the report does not say whether this was the deputy sheriff.

The Savannah Morning News carried Battersby's statement on March 21, 1903, under the headline "Why He Was Whipped," with no other version and no comment. The item referred to the whipping as having been "published" earlier, but that first report was not found, and no Black newspaper in the coverage mentioned the case. The man's guilt of false swearing therefore rests entirely on the word of an official defending the men who whipped him.
